implementation_notes: Swift's standard library provides the predicate removal as a method: RangeReplaceableCollection/MutableCollection.removeAll(where:) 'Removes all the elements that satisfy the given predicate ... The order of the remaining elements is preserved', documented as O(n); the stdlib implementation half-stable-partitions the collection in place and then calls removeSubrange once, so the tail is released in a single step exactly like the classic idiom, while the general non-mutable overload reassigns the collection to a filtered copy. filter(_:) is the copy-out alternative when the value should not be mutated in place, and removeSubrange/removeSubranges cover range- and index-set-shaped removals. Prefer removeAll(where:) on arrays and buffers whose identity is not shared, remembering that Swift's value semantics make 'in place' mean 'in place on the uniquely referenced buffer'.
code_sketch:
var numbers = [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]
numbers.removeAll(where: { $0 % 2 != 0 })   // [6, 8, 10]: order preserved, O(n)
let kept = numbers.filter { $0 > 6 }        // copy-out alternative
pitfalls: Array copy-on-write: if another variable or closure still references the array, the first mutation makes a unique copy first, so 'in place' means 'in place when uniquely referenced' - a hot loop holding a shared reference silently pays for a copy.

All indices are invalidated by the removal (the count changed), and looping over collected indices calling remove(at:) is the O(n*k) pattern - remove(at:) documents that all following elements move to close the gap; use removeSubranges or one removeAll(where:) instead.
removeAll() without a predicate (keepingCapacity:) is a different operation: it empties the collection, and keepingCapacity: true deliberately keeps the buffer alive.
